newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian dictator's widow happy after jail release.
newsitem.headline: Albanian dictator's widow happy after jail release.

text.p: Nexhmije Hoxha, widow of Albanian Stalinist dictator Enver Hoxha, spent Friday at her son's home on a former chicken farm after serving five years in prison for embezzling state cash to fund her lavish lifestyle.
Wearing a long grey coat and yellow woollen scarf, grey-haired Hoxha, 76, emerged from Tirana's top-security prison looking dignified and unscathed.
"I am very pleased to be among free people. But that pleasure is mixed with emotions, anxiety," she told reporters.
During Enver Hoxha's iron rule in Europe's poorest and most isolated state, his relatives held high-ranking posts and enjoyed privileges of which ordinary Albanians could only dream.

Hoxha ruled for four decades until his death in April 1985. Religion, private property, travel abroad, and foreign books and films were strictly forbidden under his rule. A popular uprising toppled Albanian communism in December 1990.
His widow was arrested in December 1991 and sentenced to nine years in jail in 1993 on charges of misappropriation of state funds and abuse of power.
Her sentence was reduced three times on the orders of conservative President Sali Berisha and she won a further cut after a new penal code came into effect in 1995.
When Enver Hoxha ruled, the couple lived in a large three-storey villa in Tirana guarded around the clock by soldiers. Nexhmije drove her own Fiat saloon car, now owned by the defence ministry.
This time around, the former first lady was driven in a second-hand car to her son's humble three-room home -- a converted building on a former chicken farm in a grubby Tirana suburb.

The once well-heeled widow, who used to be the second most powerful person in Albania, was happy for photographers to take her picture with the grandchildren she had missed for so long -- but only after she had slipped into a fresh set of clothes.

Nexhmije, born on February 8, 1921, to a Moslem Albanian family in present-day Macedonia, married Hoxha when she was 24. She was a founding member of the communist party and held key posts throughout its four decade-long rule.
Most Albanians, facing the challenges of a fledgling market economy, showed little interest in the Hoxha family saga.
"The communists did a lot of harm but it is humane to let her out and this would serve as a lesson of tolerance to the next generation," one pensioner said.
An electrician said he expected the Hoxha clan to leave Albania -- "They were only waiting for their mother's release and they have so much money. Why should they stay here? To be persecuted?"
"She was at the head of that clan which ruled Albania for half a century. But still I think it was a political trial with her," said a middle-aged man named Kadri.
Others felt that the people's desire for revenge for the widow's embezzlement had not been satisfied.
"Well, they kept her in jail for nothing, in vain. What did democracy win? Nothing at all," a nightwatchman said.
Hoxha said she wanted first to spend time with her children but hoped later to publish her memoirs which she wrote in jail.
